title: Qualified Personnel - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Find out why employing Qualified Personnel is a key indicator of systematic R&D investigation in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: Qualified personnel are the qualified individuals who perform an eligible SR&ED project in Canada, carrying out systematic investigation through experiment or analysis. Their directly engaged salaries and wages form the core of most federal claims, while under the Proxy Method a specified employee's salary or wages included in the salary base is capped at the lesser of 75% of that employee's total salary or wages and 2.5 × YMPE.

body.text: Qualified personnel are the qualified individuals who perform an eligible SR&ED project in Canada, carrying out systematic investigation through experiment or analysis. Their directly engaged salaries and wages form the core of most federal claims, while under the Proxy Method a specified employee's salary or wages included in the salary base is capped at the lesser of 75% of that employee's total salary or wages and 2.5 × YMPE.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Parliament and the Department of Finance Canada enacted and proposed the most sweeping structural modernization of the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program in more than a decade. Enacted through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, four core statutory enhancements now govern taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and capital property acquisitions or lease outlays after December 15, 2024): doubling the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million; expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor by 50% from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million alongside an alternative three-year average gross revenue phase-out method; extending the enhanced 35% refundable ITC beyond Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs); and reinstating SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays for both income deduction and ITC purposes. Operationally, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional eight-week Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, and issued comprehensively revised prescribed forms and administrative policies between May and October 2026.

Two further federal and provincial developments anchor 2026–2027 Canadian R&D tax planning. Federally, Budget 2026 (tabled in November 2026) proposes an additional $930 million five-year SR&ED expansion—applying prospectively to taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day—to make initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs eligible for SR&ED tax support. Because Budget 2026 measures remain proposed legislation awaiting parliamentary enactment as of mid-November 2026, claimants and auditors must separate enacted Bill C-15 law from prospective Budget 2026 proposals. Provincially, Quebec abolished its legacy suite of researcher-salary, university, consortium, pre-competitive, technology-adaptation, and industrial-design tax credits and replaced them with the unified, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)—paying 30% on up to $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization outlays above an exclusion threshold and 20% above $1 million—for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, while Saskatchewan doubled its refundable 10% R&D credit cap for CCPCs from $1 million to $2 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
Federal Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution (2024–2026)
Core Statutory Framework under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal R&D tax regime is codified within interlocking provisions of the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and sections 2900 and 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945. Rather than relying on a standalone super-deduction, the federal SR&ED program delivers two complementary statutory tax incentives to corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships carrying on qualifying work in Canada. First, claimants pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures and reinstated post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, deducting any portion of that pool to reduce net business income for the current taxation year or carrying unclaimed balances forward to offset net income in future taxation years. Second, claimants earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under subsection 127(5) and the definitions in subsection 127(9)—coupled with the cash refundability rules in section 127.1—at a basic rate of 15% or an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures. Partnerships do not pay Part I income tax directly; instead, eligible SR&ED deductions and the 15% partnership-level ITC are calculated as if the partnership were a person and allocated to qualifying members under subsections 127(8) and 127(8.2).

The technical gateway to all federal SR&ED benefits is subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which defines "scientific research and experimental development" and governs project-level eligibility across both section 37 and section 127. Section 37 establishes domestic expenditure pooling (subsection 37(1)), permits SR&ED related to a business of a related corporation (subsection 37(1.1)), distinguishes Traditional Method versus Proxy Method overhead rules (paragraph 37(8)(a)), addresses entities deriving 90% or more of revenue from prosecuting SR&ED (paragraph 37(8)(c)), and enforces mandatory reporting deadlines (subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12)). Upon a corporate amalgamation, paragraphs 87(2)(l) and 87(2)(qq) and subsection 87(2.1) deem the newly amalgamated corporation to be the same corporation as, and a continuation of, each predecessor corporation for purposes of section 37 pools, Part VIII, and computing year-end ITC balances. Within the Income Tax Regulations, section 2900 prescribes the Proxy Method mechanics and defines facility and equipment maintenance, upkeep, and incremental expenses "directly attributable" to SR&ED under subsection 2900(3), whereas section 2902 defines "prescribed expenditures"—such as employee cafeterias, clinics, recreational facilities, non-SR&ED facility maintenance, and used capital equipment—that are barred from earning an ITC under subsection 127(9) even where deductible under section 37.

body.text: Enacted Reforms under Bill C-15 (Statutes of Canada 2026, c. 3)

The legislative overhaul currently in force originated in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled December 16, 2024) and was broadened in Budget 2025: Canada Strong (tabled November 4, 2025), which elevated the proposed enhanced expenditure limit from an interim proposal to $6 million. Introduced for First Reading on November 18, 2025 during the 1st Session of the 45th Parliament as Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), the legislation cleared House of Commons report-stage votes on February 25, 2026, passed the Senate, and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, becoming Chapter 3 of the Statutes of Canada 2026.

Auditors and corporate tax departments must distinguish two statutory transition rules enacted in Bill C-15. First, the structural enhancements to credit eligibility and thresholds—doubling the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million, widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds by 50% from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million (reflecting cumulative inflation since those thresholds were last adjusted in 2008), introducing the three-year average gross revenue phase-out method, and extending the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations—apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Accordingly, a calendar-year taxpayer's 2024 return remained governed by the legacy $3 million CCPC-only limit, whereas its 2025 and 2026 returns qualify in full under the enacted Bill C-15 regime. Department of Finance Canada briefing materials estimate that roughly 550 CCPCs directly benefit from the higher expenditure limit and broadened taxable capital phase-out corridor alone.

Second, the reinstatement of SR&ED capital expenditures (which had been repealed for property acquired after 2013) and equipment lease costs operates on a transaction-date cutoff rather than a taxation-year-start cutoff: depreciable property must be acquired after December 15, 2024 (and available for use after that date under subsection 37(1.2)), and equipment lease outlays must be incurred or first become payable after December 15, 2024. Where a corporation's taxation year began before December 16, 2024 and straddled that date, capital property acquired before December 16, 2024 remains permanently excluded, whereas qualifying property acquired or equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 are eligible within that straddle year—with SR&ED equipment operating-time percentages measured across total operating time in the post-December 15, 2024 portion of the transition year.
Proposed Expansion in Federal Budget 2026 (November 2026)

On top of the enacted Bill C-15 reforms, Budget 2026 (tax measures updated November 5, 2026) proposes a further $930 million five-year expansion of the SR&ED program over fiscal years 2026–2027 through 2030–2031. As of mid-November 2026, these Budget 2026 measures represent proposed tax legislation rather than enacted statute and are scheduled to apply prospectively to taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day.

The first pillar of the Budget 2026 proposal brings regulatory and certification requirements into the scope of eligible SR&ED work. Specifically, tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process will qualify, provided those activities directly relate to an underlying project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules. All expenditure categories recognized under existing SR&ED rules—including wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment—will qualify when incurred for eligible regulatory validation work.

The second pillar expands eligible SR&ED expenditures to encompass intellectual property (IP) protection costs incurred to register and maintain protection for IP developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project. Qualifying IP instruments are strictly limited to four statutory categories registered or protected under Canadian legislation or equivalent legislation in another jurisdiction: patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. Covered outlays comprise expenses reasonably incurred to prepare and file applications for an eligible form of IP protection together with periodic maintenance fees payable to keep those IP rights in force. Budget 2026 proposes three explicit exclusions plus a clawback rule: costs incurred to enforce IP rights (such as infringement litigation) are ineligible; outlays not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights are excluded; and supporting professional activities (such as preparing a patent application) conducted outside Canada are disallowed, although official administrative fees paid to a foreign IP office remain eligible. Finally, recapture rules will apply to claw back related SR&ED income deductions and ITC amounts if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED IP-protection support was claimed.

body.text: Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryovers
Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Structure

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and the CRA's revised SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (published October 7, 2026), federal SR&ED ITCs are earned at either an enhanced 35% rate or a basic 15% rate. The enhanced 35% ITC (representing the 15% basic specified percentage plus a 20% statutory enhancement) applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the claimant's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, access to the 35% rate was restricted exclusively to CCPCs up to a maximum expenditure limit of $3,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit is doubled to $6,000,000—enabling up to $2,100,000 in annual enhanced credits, an increase of $1,050,000 per year—and eligibility is extended to both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). An ECPC is defined as a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange that is resident in Canada and is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by non-resident persons. Extending the 35% rate to ECPCs eliminates the sharp drop in tax support that Canadian private innovators previously suffered when completing an initial public offering on a designated stock exchange.

The basic 15% ITC applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC above its annual expenditure limit, as well as to all qualified SR&ED expenditures of every other claimant category—including foreign-controlled private corporations, public corporations controlled by non-residents or exceeding the $75 million average revenue ceiling, individuals and sole proprietorships, trusts, and members of partnerships. Where a claimant repays government assistance or a contract payment that previously reduced qualified expenditures in an earlier taxation year, the ITC earned on that repayment is computed using the specified percentage and additional enhanced rate that applied in the prior taxation year in which the assistance or contract payment was originally received.

Two mandatory sharing and proration rules prevent multiplication of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Whenever a CCPC or ECPC has a short taxation year of less than 51 weeks, its expenditure limit must be prorated using the formula Expenditure Limit × (Number of days in the taxation year ÷ 365). Furthermore, associated CCPCs must share and allocate a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit across all members of the associated group using prescribed Schedule T2SCH49 (revised May 29, 2026), while ECPCs belonging to a corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit across all members of the consolidated group.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Regimes: Taxable Capital Method vs. Gross Revenue Method

To retain SME targeting while allowing domestic scale-ups to grow without prematurely losing enhanced R&D support, the post-December 15, 2024 statutory regime establishes two distinct phase-out methods over an identical $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 corridor.

Under the Taxable Capital Method—the default statutory test for CCPCs—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins phasing out when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs in the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is reduced to nil ($0) once prior-year combined taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (up from the pre-December 16, 2024 thresholds of $10,000,000 and $50,000,000).

Under the Gross Revenue Method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins phasing out when average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years reaches or exceeds $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) once three-year average annual gross revenue reaches or exceeds $75,000,000. For ECPCs, the Gross Revenue Method applies automatically and exclusively, calculated from the average annual revenue reported in the consolidated financial statements of the consolidated group over the preceding three fiscal years. Critically, CCPCs may also elect to use the Gross Revenue Method on a prescribed form instead of the Taxable Capital Method. This election provides substantial tax relief for capital-intensive, pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPCs (such as biotechnology, quantum computing, or clean-energy ventures) whose balance-sheet equity financings push taxable capital above $15 million or $75 million while three-year average revenue remains modest. If an electing CCPC belongs to an associated group, all associated CCPCs must jointly file the election, and group revenue aggregates financial-statement revenue across all group members for the three preceding fiscal years (regardless of whether they were associated throughout that entire three-year period), plus proportionate shares of partnership and trust revenues, with adjustments permitted for intra-group transactions.
Entity-by-Entity Refundability Matrix (Current vs. Capital Expenditures)

Earned SR&ED ITCs must first be applied against Part I federal income tax payable to reduce income tax to zero. Any unused current-year ITC balance may then be paid out as a direct cash refund under section 127.1 depending on the claimant's classification, whether the expenditures lie within or above the expenditure limit, and whether the outlays are current expenditures or reinstated post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures. Within the CCPC category, the statute distinguishes a Qualifying Corporation—defined as a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income (combined with any associated corporations) did not exceed its qualifying income limit for the current year—from an Excluded Corporation and from other CCPCs whose prior-year taxable income exceeded their qualifying income limit. Notably, both non-excluded CCPCs above their qualifying income limit and ECPCs still earn 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures up to their $6,000,000 expenditure limit; however, only Qualifying Corporations (and Excluded Corporations) earn a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC above the expenditure limit.

body.text: Pool Carryforwards, ITC Carryovers, Acquisition of Control, and Recapture

Balances accumulated in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in the current taxation year or carried forward to reduce net income in future taxation years. Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs—after deducting amounts applied against Part I tax payable and amounts refunded in cash—may be carried back up to 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years. Where a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, statutory loss-streaming rules restrict both the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control.

To ensure SR&ED tax incentives subsidize only the net economic cost of R&D assets and materials, statutory ITC recapture applies whenever materials transformed during SR&ED, or depreciable capital property acquired before 2014 or after December 15, 2024 for which a qualified SR&ED expenditure was claimed, are sold or converted to commercial use. Recapture adds back all or a portion of the previously earned SR&ED ITC directly to the claimant's Part I income tax payable in the taxation year in which the sale or commercial conversion occurs, calculated and reported on Schedule T2SCH31 (corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (individuals and partnership members). Additionally, because deductions for SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) are deemed Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), disposing of SR&ED depreciable property may also trigger regular CCA recapture (referenced at Line 440 of Form T661).
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures, Overhead Methods, and Capital/Lease Reinstatement
Technical Eligibility Criteria and Project-Level Boundaries

Financial outlays qualify for section 37 pooling and section 127 ITCs only where the underlying technical work meets the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED as interpreted in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (published August 13, 2021) and Guide T4088. An eligible SR&ED project comprises a set of interrelated activities that are collectively necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements, pursued through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals. It encompasses basic research, applied research, and experimental development, and CRA project-level eligibility reviews encompass all directly required support work necessary for the attempted scientific or technological advancement.

In audit practice, CRA Research and Technology Advisors enforce strict boundaries on measurable scientific methodology and commercial production overlaps. First, CRA guidance warns that if a study's end results cannot be measured or counted, the work may fail to qualify as SR&ED. Second, where experimental development takes place concurrently with industrial trials or shop-floor manufacturing, the CRA's Production Runs Policy distinguishes runs combining experimental development with experimental production (ED+EP) from runs combining experimental development with commercial production (ED+CP, the default classification where a production run is not strictly ED+EP). Third, under section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations and section 127 definitions, outlays for facility/equipment maintenance not attributable to prosecuting scientific research, employee cafeterias, clinics, and recreational facilities, and preliminary mining test-pit or trench sampling are excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures.
Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and Materials

Directly engaged employee salaries and wages for SR&ED work performed in Canada form the core expenditure base of most claims, governed by the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy. Special regulatory limits apply to Specified Employees reported on Form T661 Line 305 (Specified employees for work performed in Canada). Under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations, when computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method, the SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee that may be included cannot exceed the lesser of 75% of that employee's total salary or wages for the year and 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), prorated for the number of days in the year the employee was employed by the claimant. Associated corporations employing the same specified employee must allocate that specified-employee salary cap among the group using the prescribed Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED (updated December 4, 2023). Eligible materials also enter current SR&ED expenditures, subject to ITC recapture if materials transformed in an SR&ED project are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.
Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (55% Prescribed Proxy Amount)

Under paragraph 37(8)(a) of the ITA and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy (updated March 30, 2022), claimants select either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method on Form T661 to account for SR&ED overhead expenditures for the taxation year.

Claimants choosing the Proxy Method do not include overhead outlays in their subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (deducting ordinary business overhead instead under general income computation rules); in exchange, they calculate a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of their eligible SR&ED salary base (subject to the specified-employee 75% and 2.5 × YMPE caps and the overall cap in Regulation 2900). Under paragraph (b) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), the 55% PPA is deemed a qualified expenditure incurred in the year for ITC computation purposes, frequently yielding a larger ITC base than actual overhead while avoiding granular overhead tracking.

Claimants choosing the Traditional Method skip Part 5 PPA and overall-cap calculations and instead specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate actual overhead and other current SR&ED expenditures (claimed on Line 360 of Form T661) for inclusion in both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures. Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) of the ITA and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, Traditional Method overhead must either be all or substantially all (≥90%) attributable to SR&ED or be "directly attributable"—meaning (a) maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment, or (b) incremental outlays directly related to that provision that would not have been incurred had those SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment not existed.

body.text: Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Non-Arm's-Length Transfers

External R&D contracts and collaborative payments are governed by the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy and Third-Party Payments Policy (both updated March 30, 2022). When a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf, 100% of the eligible contract outlay is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, but only 80% enters "qualified expenditures" under subparagraph (a)(ii) of that definition in subsection 127(9) for ITC calculation. Conversely, for the Canadian contractor performing the R&D, an amount received or receivable from a "taxable supplier" for SR&ED performed at arm's length on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to a section 37 deduction—or payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or section 149 tax-exempt entity—constitutes a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), reducing the contractor's own qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) so that two Canadian entities cannot claim ITCs on the same work.

Third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii)) fund SR&ED carried on in Canada where the claimant does not direct a bilateral subcontract, provided the SR&ED relates to a business of the claimant and the claimant gains the legal right to exploit the results of that SR&ED. Eligible payees comprise A entities (corporations resident in Canada) and B to E entities—specifically including B entities (approved associations), C entities (approved universities, colleges, and research institutes), and D entities (non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j)), alongside specialized rules for agricultural producer check-off dues directed to B, C, or D entities. Qualifying third-party payments are exempt from the general prepaid-expense limitation of paragraph 18(9)(a) pursuant to paragraph 18(9)(d) (though if a payment is invested so only investment income funds SR&ED, only the principal portion specified in the written agreement for SR&ED qualifies), and 80% of the eligible payment enters qualified expenditures for ITC purposes.

Where SR&ED is performed by a non-arm's-length (NAL) party, paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) excludes the payer's contract payment from earning an ITC directly. Instead, the NAL performer computes its own underlying SR&ED qualified expenditures and may transfer them to the NAL payer using prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, revised May 15, 2026). Under the ITA, the performer cannot transfer more than its year-end qualified expenditure balance—if it attempts to transfer an excess amount, the statute voids the entire transfer so that zero is transferred—and partnerships cannot transfer or receive amounts on Form T1146 because a partnership is not a "person" under those provisions. Finally, while former subsections 37(14) and 37(15) imposed a "capital look-through rule" between 2014 and December 15, 2024 requiring contract and third-party payers to deduct any capital or lease outlays incurred by the performer (with mandatory 90-day written notice from the performer), that disallowance applies only to capital outlays made before December 16, 2024.
Reinstated SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (published June 29, 2026) and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (published May 22, 2026), depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (subject to the available-for-use rule in subsection 37(1.2)) qualifies through two statutory routes.

First, depreciable property owned by the claimant (or deemed acquired at fair market value with a matching deemed loan via a joint lessor-lessee election under section 16.1 of the ITA) qualifies as a full SR&ED capital expenditure under paragraph 37(1)(b) (claimed on Line 390 of Form T661) if acquired with the intent either to (1) use the property all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (2) consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Capital cost encompasses full acquisition costs including purchase price, installation, customs and excise duties, and transportation; for self-manufactured equipment, it includes reasonably attributable material, labour, and overhead without notional profit. Assets claimed on Line 390 receive a 100% write-off in the subsection 37(1) pool (deemed CCA) and must be excluded from Schedule T2SCH8 (regular CCA). Auditors must enforce two strict exclusions on Line 390 claims: non-depreciable assets (such as land), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings do not qualify; and while used depreciable equipment meeting the ≥90% ASA test is deductible in the section 37 pool on Line 390, used equipment is a "prescribed expenditure" under Regulation 2902 that must be backed out on Line 532 of Form T661 so that it earns zero SR&ED ITC.

Second, capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 that do not satisfy the ≥90% ASA threshold may still earn SR&ED ITCs as "first term shared-use-equipment" or "second term shared-use-equipment" (Shared-Use Equipment / SUE, claimed on Line 504 of Form T661) under subsection 127(9) and the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (published May 22, 2026). The SUE ITC calculation is identical under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, and unlike ASA capital property on Line 390, the capital cost of SUE does not enter the subsection 37(1) SR&ED pool—meaning the claimant depreciates SUE under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8 while claiming the SUE ITC via Line 504.
Reinstated SR&ED Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024) and Unpaid Amounts (180-Day Rule)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (published June 8, 2026), equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024 are evaluated across the entire taxation year: a claimant cannot isolate a two- or three-month spike of high SR&ED usage within a 12-month taxation year to claim primary or ASA status, though transition years straddling December 16, 2024 measure SR&ED operating time solely over total operating time after December 15, 2024. Under the Proxy Method, equipment leased and used ≥90% (ASA) of operating time for SR&ED is 100% claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), equipment used >50% and <90% (primarily) is 50% claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), equipment used ≤50% is 0% claimable, and general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) and land leases are barred. Under the Traditional Method, equipment (including GPOEF) leased and used ≥90% (ASA) is 100% claimable as a lease cost, while equipment leased and used <90% may be claimed proportionally on Line 360 as overhead provided it is directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to SR&ED. Under both methods, building rent is strictly disallowed—save only for post-December 15, 2024 leases of prescribed special-purpose buildings approved on a building-by-building basis by the Department of Finance Canada—requiring mixed building-and-equipment leases to be reasonably allocated, whereas engineering structures (such as bridges or dams) are not buildings and can qualify under Traditional or Proxy rules.

Separately, subsection 127(26) of the ITA enforces a strict 180-day unpaid amounts cutoff: any current SR&ED expenditure (paragraph 37(1)(a)) remaining unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is excluded from qualified expenditures for that year (subsections 127(5) to 127(25) and section 127.1) and added to qualified expenditures only in the subsequent taxation year when paid (at 80% if subject to the contract/third-party haircut).
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentives Across Canada

Nine provinces and Yukon provide corporate (and in Newfoundland and Labrador and Yukon, individual) R&D tax credits or tax-administered grants that stack alongside federal SR&ED, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut provide no provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. All provincial and territorial R&D credits—except Quebec's Revenu Québec-administered CRIC and Alberta's AT1-administered Innovation Employment Grant—are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency. Because provincial and territorial R&D credits constitute "government assistance" under federal subsection 127(9), they reduce both the federal subsection 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures and federal qualified expenditures unless formally renounced/waived by the income tax return filing-due date.

body.text: Quebec: The Unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

Effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec fundamentally restructured its R&D tax system by creating the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) and eliminating its legacy suite of R&D and design credits—specifically abolishing the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers, the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, and the industrial design component of the design tax credits (an overhaul characterized in an industry funding guide as replacing eight prior Quebec measures). For most calendar-year corporations, 2026 represents their first taxation year governed by the CRIC.

Claimed with Revenu Québec on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR) by any corporation operating a business and maintaining an establishment in Quebec (regardless of foreign or public ownership), the CRIC delivers a 100% refundable credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier. Beyond basic research, applied research, and experimental development (including incremental improvements), the CRIC covers two categories of pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec in conjunction with Quebec R&D: (1) regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies aimed at obtaining initial commercialization approval or certification, and (2) product design, including form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials.

Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible Quebec R&D and pre-commercialization work, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Quebec, 50% of payments to an eligible public research centre, research consortium, or university entity, and property acquisition costs—excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property covered by an initial qualification certificate for a large investment project tax holiday. Before applying the 30% and 20% rates, qualified expenditures must exceed an applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the personal income tax basic personal amount for each R&D and pre-commercialization employee prorated for time devoted to eligible activities. As noted in advisory guidance, an expense claimed under CRIC generally cannot be double-claimed under other Quebec credits such as the C3i investment credit. Alongside CRIC, Quebec's Budget Plan also maintains the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI).
Ontario, Western Canada, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon Nuances

In Ontario, corporations combine up to three CRA-administered credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario): the 8% refundable OITC (up to a $3,000,000 expenditure limit; previously 10% for tax years ending before June 1, 2016), the 20% refundable OBRITC on eligible contracts with Eligible Research Institutes up to a $20,000,000 group cap (excluding payments funding ERI employees connected to the payer), and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule T2SCH508, previously 4.5% before June 1, 2016; plus transitional schedules T2SCH506 and T2SCH507). Because claiming a non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC immediately reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures—costing a Qualifying CCPC or ECPC 35 cents on the dollar in refundable federal cash credits—loss-making Ontario corporations frequently waive all or part of their current-year ORDTC under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) on or before their T2 filing-due date. Similar statutory renunciation elections exist in British Columbia (subsection 100(1) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act for the non-refundable portion of BC's permanent 10% credit on Form T666) and Manitoba (subsection 7.3(7) of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) for the non-refundable 7.5% half of Manitoba's 15% in-house R&D credit on Schedule T2SCH380).

In Alberta, where the 8% general corporate income tax rate is the lowest in Canada, the provincial Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, ss. 26.95–26.99; AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970; Information Circular IEG-1) rewards R&D growth on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta SR&ED-aligned spending incurred after December 31, 2020: corporations receive an 8% refundable payment up to their two-year rolling average Alberta R&D spending base and a 20% refundable payment on incremental spending above that base, claimed within 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date. Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403) doubled its 10% refundable CCPC expenditure cap from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, while retaining a 10% non-refundable credit above that limit and for non-CCPCs up to a combined $1,000,000 annual credit ceiling (historically 15% prior to April 2015). Across New Brunswick (T2SCH360), Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador (T2SCH301 / T1129), and Yukon (T2SCH442 / T1232), claimants earn 15% fully refundable R&D credits without an upper expenditure cap, with Yukon adding a 5% refundable bonus (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.
Government Assistance, Innovation Grants, and Tax-Credit Stacking Mechanics
Direct Federal Innovation Funding and Statutory Assistance Reductions

Canadian R&D performers regularly stack statutory SR&ED credits with direct federal innovation contributions led by the National Research Council of Canada's Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP)—including specialized initiatives such as NRC-IRAP's AI Assist program and its consolidated Concierge Service—and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (alongside provincial counterparts such as Alberta Innovates AICE, noted in funding guides as covering up to 75% of eligible costs up to $300,000–$600,000).

Under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, all government assistance (including direct grants, provincial/territorial R&D tax credits not validly renounced by the filing-due date, and public-authority funding) and non-government assistance that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax filing-due date reduces both the subsection 37(1) pool and subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures. Notably, under the statutory ordering in subsection 127(9), "qualified expenditure" first aggregates current, contract (80%), SUE, and capital outlays in paragraph (a) together with the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in paragraph (b), and then applies subsection 127(18)–(20) assistance reductions in paragraph (h). Where assistance and contract payments on a project exceed a performer's SR&ED outlays in a non-arm's-length relationship (subsection 127(19)), excess assistance may be allocated among related parties using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, revised May 15, 2026; reported by the transferee on Form T661 Line 540), filed by the transferor's return filing-due date or within its notice-of-objection window.
Worked Tax Audit Calculations: Post-Bill C-15 Federal and Quebec CRIC Stacking
Case Study 1: Enacted Bill C-15 Impact on a Qualifying CCPC and an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (2026 Tax Year)

Consider a Canadian R&D corporation (taxation year January 1, 2026 – December 31, 2026; prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada = $9,500,000; three-year average consolidated gross revenue = $14,000,000; $0 Part I tax payable) electing the Proxy Method and incurring the following Canadian SR&ED outlays (assuming a jurisdiction without provincial credits or where non-refundable provincial credits are waived): $3,000,000 in directly engaged arm's-length R&D salaries, $500,000 to an arm's-length Canadian SR&ED subcontractor, $800,000 on March 1, 2026 for new depreciable SR&ED test machinery used 95% (≥90% ASA) of operating time over its expected useful life, and $200,000 in direct federal R&D grant assistance received for current project outlays.

items: Capital Qualified Expenditures (new ≥90% ASA depreciable property acquired after Dec 15, 2024): $800,000.

Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures: $4,850,000 + $800,000 = $5,650,000 (fully inside the $6,000,000 expenditure limit because both $9.5M taxable capital and $14.0M average revenue lie below the $15,000,000 phase-out floor).
Federal SR&ED ITC and Refund Calculation (Identical for Qualifying CCPC or ECPC):
Enhanced ITC on current expenditures: $4,850,000 × 35% = $1,697,500 → 100% refundable = $1,697,500 cash refund.

Enhanced ITC on capital expenditures: $800,000 × 35% = $280,000 → 40% refundable = $280,000 × 40% = $112,000 cash refund, plus $168,000 non-refundable ITC carryback (3 years) / carryforward (20 years).
Total Federal ITC Earned: $1,977,500, delivering $1,809,500 in immediate cash refund.

body.text: Case Study 2: Quebec CRIC Calculation and Federal Stacking (2026 Tax Year)

Suppose a Quebec corporation (taxation year January 1, 2026 – December 31, 2026, beginning after March 25, 2025) incurs $1,200,000 in Quebec R&D and pre-commercialization salaries, $400,000 in Quebec R&D subcontractor invoices, and $300,000 for eligible new R&D equipment in Quebec, with an employee-adjusted basic personal amount exclusion threshold of $120,000 (exceeding the $50,000 minimum):

items: Gross Quebec CRIC Qualified Expenditures: $1,200,000 (100% salaries) + $200,000 (50% of $400,000 subcontractor) + $300,000 (100% equipment) = $1,700,000.

Federal SR&ED Assistance Adjustment: On federal Form T661, the portion of the $416,000 CRIC attributable to federal-eligible SR&ED current and post-December 15, 2024 capital outlays (with provincial capital assistance entered on Line 514) reduces the federal pool and federal qualified expenditures before applying the 35% or 15% federal ITC.

body.text: Governance, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Procedures, Audits, and Jurisprudence
Governing Authorities, Optional Pre-Claim Approval, and 2026 Policy Updates

Tax policy and statutory amendments are overseen by the Department of Finance Canada, while operational administration, technical eligibility reviews, and financial audits are conducted by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through specialized SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), storing T2 claim data on CORTAX and T1 claim data on RAPID. On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process, allowing businesses to submit up to three proposed SR&ED projects before starting work to obtain an upfront eligibility determination within eight weeks, with each project approval valid for up to three years. Pre-claim approval is optional, and approved businesses must still submit a full year-end SR&ED claim—checking Line 212 and entering their assigned pre-claim approval case number on Line 214 of Form T661. In Fall 2026, the CRA also announced upgrades to the SR&ED Client Portal and Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT).

body.text: Form T661 Compliance, Claim Preparer Penalties, and Hard Statutory Deadlines

Electronic filing via CRA-approved commercial software is mandatory for most corporations. On the May 15, 2026 revision of Form T661, claimants must report a 5-digit Field of Research code (RDF#####) from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 on Line 207, provide concise word-limited technical narratives in Part 2, Section B authored in technical language by personnel familiar with the work, and—where claiming post-December 15, 2024 capital property on Line 390—enter the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties per project on Line 262 and their SR&ED operating-time percentages on Line 263. In Part 9, claimants using any external fee-paid advisor (excluding an employee acting within employment duties) must report complete "claim preparer information"—covering (a) the claim preparer's identity and (b) the arrangement under which the preparer agrees to accept consideration. Missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 disclosures trigger a $1,000 civil penalty under subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally liable, and claimants remain legally liable—including for gross negligence penalties on overstated claims—even if misled by third-party promoters.

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA and the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, prescribed forms containing complete prescribed expenditure and ITC information must be filed no later than 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date under subsection 150(1). Submitting a letter expressing "an intent to file" or partially completed forms missing prescribed fields does not satisfy the statute. Missing the SR&ED reporting deadline permanently bars section 37 SR&ED deductions and ITCs on those outlays (subsection 37(12)), while filing Form T661 on time without filing Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) by the deadline preserves the section 37 income deduction pool but permanently forfeits all ITCs.

body.text: Judicial Precedents, Audit Reviews, and Contemporaneous Documentation Checklist
To substantiate claims during combined CRA Technical and Financial Reviews, claimants should maintain the following contemporaneous records for every project:

items: Systematic Investigation Records: Dated technical specifications, experimental hypotheses, test protocols, analytical logs, and measurable or countable test outcomes establishing scientific or technological uncertainty and advancement.

Employee Time-Tracking & Payroll Support: Contemporaneous time records linking directly engaged personnel (including Specified Employees subject to the Proxy Method 75% and 2.5 × YMPE salary-base caps) to specific SR&ED projects in Canada.

Capital & Lease Operating-Time Logbooks: Full-year equipment logbooks documenting SR&ED operating hours relative to total operating hours across the entire taxation year to substantiate ≥90% ASA capital deductions on Line 390, Shared-Use Equipment ITCs on Line 504, and post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease percentages.

Contracts, Third-Party Rights & 180-Day Payment Proof: Executed subcontractor agreements, lease contracts, written third-party agreements proving the claimant's right to exploit SR&ED results, invoices, and cancelled cheques or payment confirmations verifying settlement within 180 days after taxation year-end under subsection 127(26).
